screens.title: Querying Data with SELECT
screens.narratorSegment: Retrieving data is the most frequent operation in many applications, and Cassandra uses the SELECT statement for this purpose. But although CQL looks like S Q L, its execution model is different: every efficient query must be expressed around the primary key so the cluster knows which partitions to read. In this lesson you will learn core SELECT patterns: why you should avoid table scans, how the WHERE clause ties to partition and clustering keys, when ORDER BY is allowed, and the real cost of ALLOW FILTERING. You will also see how LIMIT and PER PARTITION LIMIT behave differently, and where a secondary index might help — and when it will hurt. By the end you should be comfortable writing SELECT statements that return only the data you need without destabilizing the cluster. A quick question to hold while we dive in: when you request rows without a partition key, what costs do you expect the coordinator node to bear?

screens.title: SELECT basics and the danger of SELECT *
screens.narratorSegment: A SELECT statement in Cassandra may look like S Q L, but its performance characteristics are different because data is partitioned across nodes. The simplest form, SELECT * FROM keyspace. table, returns every column and every row unless you constrain it. In distributed clusters this causes a full table scan: each node must contribute rows and the coordinator collects and streams them, which can saturate network and C P U. For this reason, production queries should never use SELECT * across large tables. Instead, pick the columns you need and provide a partition key so Cassandra targets a single partition. For example, selecting a blog post by its post_id is efficient because the coordinator reads only that partition: SELECT title, content FROM user_profiles. blog_posts WHERE post_id = /* your_post_id */; A common misconception is that SELECT * is harmless for infrequent queries; in reality the coordinator can still touch many nodes and lead to timeouts. Another subtle point is that selecting fewer columns reduces payload size and lowers read amplification. As a practical rule, design your application query to return only the fields required for the user story. Reflect: if a query must scan many partitions, how would you remodel the data to avoid that scan?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Avoid SELECT * on large tables. Always target partitions and select only needed columns to prevent cluster strain.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › SELECT basics
Core Concept

SELECT basics

CQL SELECT retrieves rows from tables. But without partition targeting, it becomes a costly cluster-wide operation.

Example query
SELECT * FROM user_profiles.users;

-- Preferred: select columns and partition key
SELECT username, email FROM user_profiles.users
WHERE user_id = 92a7f0e0-5a3b-4c8d-8e1f-2b6c7d8e9f0a;
Common mistake

Using SELECT * for convenience leads to unpredictable load and long-running reads. It is not a safe production pattern.

Key takeaway

Pick columns and supply the partition key. That is the fastest, most stable approach.

Explanation & impact
  • SELECT * forces the coordinator to fetch data from many nodes, increasing latency and resource use.
  • Selecting specific columns reduces I/O and network payload sizes between replicas and coordinator.
  • Targeting the full partition key allows Cassandra to route the read to the correct replicas efficiently.
  • When in doubt, model a table specifically for the read pattern rather than scanning with SELECT *.
Practice prompt

Review an application endpoint that needs multiple fields across many rows. Could you return a smaller column set or create a narrow table keyed by that access pattern?

screens.title: WHERE clause rules and the partition key requirement
screens.narratorSegment: The WHERE clause in CQL is tightly coupled to the primary key. Cassandra requires the full partition key to be present in the WHERE clause for efficient queries; without it, the coordinator cannot narrow the read to a known partition and will either fail or require ALLOW FILTERING. Think of the partition key as the address of a house in a distributed neighborhood: you must give the house number to fetch its contents quickly. You can filter on clustering columns after supplying the partition key, and clustering filters must follow the column order defined in the table schema. Supported operators include equality, IN for multiple partition values, and range operators for clustering columns. For example, selecting comments for a post by post_id is correct, and you can apply a time range on the clustering comment_id using > and minTimeuuid('2023-01-01') AND comment_id < maxTimeuuid('2024-01-01'); A frequent misconception is that IN on a partition key is always free; while IN lets you read multiple partitions, it causes multiple partition reads and may still be expensive if many partitions are involved. Ask yourself: am I targeting a small, bounded set of partitions, or am I requesting a broad scan?

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Always include the full partition key in WHERE. Use clustering column filters only after the partition is fixed and in defined order.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › WHERE clause rules
Process Flow

Partition key first, clustering next

Provide the full partition key so Cassandra targets the correct replicas. Apply clustering filters after that and in the order defined by the schema.

Step 1 — Identify partition key
Ensure WHERE specifies every column that composes the partition key.
Step 2 — Apply clustering filters
Use equality or range operators on clustering columns in their defined sequence to slice within the partition.
Step 3 — Avoid broad INs
IN on partition key reads multiple partitions; it's fine for a small set but costly at scale.
Concrete example
-- Select comments for a given post, with time-range on clustering column
SELECT comment_text, created_at FROM user_profiles.post_comments
WHERE post_id = /* your_post_id */
AND comment_id > minTimeuuid('2023-01-01 00:00:00+0000')
AND comment_id < maxTimeuuid('2024-01-01 00:00:00+0000');
Misconception

People sometimes expect arbitrary column filtering to work like SQL. In Cassandra, that only works if the column is part of the primary key or indexed — otherwise the query will error or require ALLOW FILTERING.

Key Takeaway

Full partition keys unlock efficient reads; clustering columns let you slice data inside that partition.

screens.title: ALLOW FILTERING: ad-hoc rescue or production anti-pattern?
screens.narratorSegment: ALLOW FILTERING lets you override Cassandra's protections and run queries that would otherwise error because they require scanning multiple partitions or filtering non-key columns. It does what it promises: it forces the coordinator to collect candidate rows from replicas and apply the filter in memory or on the coordinator, but that comes at a cost — increased network traffic, coordinator C P U load, and unpredictable latency. Use ALLOW FILTERING only for ad-hoc investigation or administrative checks on small tables. For application queries, prefer modelling your data for the required access pattern or using a secondary index when appropriate. A concrete example: querying users by city with ALLOW FILTERING will work but can scan many partitions. Better approaches include adding city to the primary key of a denormalized table used specifically for that query, or creating a carefully chosen secondary index when cardinality is suitable. A persistent misconception is to accept occasional slow queries with ALLOW FILTERING; in real deployments, occasional slow queries often become consistent problems under load. Before adding ALLOW FILTERING, ask whether a schema change or index would serve the query safely.

keyIdea.text: ALLOW FILTERING enables hard queries but is usually unsafe for production. Prefer modeling or indexes over filtering at read time.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › ALLOW FILTERING
Comparison

ALLOW FILTERING vs model change

  • ALLOW FILTERING: immediate, may scan many partitions, useful for small ad-hoc checks.
  • Schema refactor: upfront cost, returns predictable, scalable reads for production traffic.
  • Secondary index: middle ground for selective, low-volume queries; has write and maintenance costs.
Example ALLOW FILTERING
SELECT username, email FROM user_profiles.users
WHERE city = 'New York' ALLOW FILTERING;
Why it matters

ALLOW FILTERING can destabilize a cluster when used for production queries. It is an emergency tool, not a pattern.

Better alternatives
  • Create a denormalized table with the desired partition key for the query pattern.
  • When appropriate, add a secondary index only for low-volume or low-cardinality values.
  • Use PER PARTITION LIMIT or LIMIT when you can bound the read size instead of scanning everything.
Warning

ALLOW FILTERING may cause coordinator-side filtering of many partitions. Use it only for small, controlled operations.

screens.title: ORDER BY: sorting only inside a partition
screens.narratorSegment: ORDER BY in Cassandra is intentionally limited: you can only sort by clustering columns and the order must respect the clustering order defined when the table was created. This restriction exists because data within a partition is physically stored according to clustering order; Cassandra can sort efficiently inside that partition, but it cannot sort across partitions without a coordination-heavy shuffle. For example, ordering post_comments by comment_id descending is valid if the clustering column is comment_id and the table's clustering order allows it: SELECT comment_text, created_at FROM user_profiles. post_comments WHERE post_id = /* id */ ORDER BY comment_id DESC; If you try to order by a non-clustering column or by a clustering column out of its defined sequence, Cassandra will return an error. A common misconception is that ORDER BY will reorganize results globally; instead, it only guarantees order within a single partition. If your application needs global ordering across partitions, you must implement an application-side aggregator or design a table keyed to the ordering you need. Consider whether you can limit results per partition and then merge them in the application, or refactor the schema for the target query.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › ORDER BY
Definition

ORDER BY inside a partition

You can sort results only by clustering columns and only in ways the table's clustering order allows. This keeps sorting efficient and local to replicas for that partition.

SELECT comment_text, created_at FROM user_profiles.post_comments
WHERE post_id = /* your_post_id */
ORDER BY comment_id DESC;
Why it matters
Efficient ordering avoids expensive sorts across nodes and keeps latency low for time-ordered feeds.
Misconception
ORDER BY does not create a global sorted set across partitions. For global sorting, you need different modeling or client-side merge.
Checklist
  • Confirm clustering column used by ORDER BY.
  • Confirm clustering order in table definition supports requested direction.
  • Prefer LIMIT to restrict result size after ordering.
Key Takeaway

ORDER BY is safe and efficient only when it sorts within a single partition according to clustering order.

screens.title: LIMIT and PER PARTITION LIMIT
screens.narratorSegment: LIMIT and PER PARTITION LIMIT let you bound the number of rows returned by a SELECT, but they serve different needs. LIMIT restricts the total number of rows in the result set, so when you query a single partition, LIMIT provides a simple top-N behavior. PER PARTITION LIMIT is specifically useful when a query touches multiple partitions, for example when you use IN on the partition key. PER PARTITION LIMIT guarantees at most N rows per partition, which helps ensure fair representation across partitions and prevents one large partition from dominating results. For example, SELECT * FROM user_profiles. post_comments WHERE post_id IN (id1, id2) PER PARTITION LIMIT 2 returns at most two comments for each post. A misconception is to treat PER PARTITION LIMIT as a global LIMIT; it is not. Also remember that combining ORDER BY with LIMIT works within a partition to return the top N in the requested order. When designing APIs, choose which of these limits matches the user story: a single global top-N across many partitions requires additional client-side aggregation, while PER PARTITION LIMIT keeps pagination predictable and partition-local.

keyIdea.text: Use LIMIT for total rows and PER PARTITION LIMIT to bound rows returned from each partition accessed by the query.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › LIMIT vs PER PARTITION LIMIT
Process Flow

How to choose a limit

  • LIMIT caps the total rows returned for the entire query.
  • PER PARTITION LIMIT caps rows returned from each partition involved.
  • Use PER PARTITION LIMIT when using IN for many partition keys to get balanced samples.
-- Top 5 comments for a single post
SELECT * FROM user_profiles.post_comments
WHERE post_id = /* id */
LIMIT 5;

-- At most 2 comments per post when querying multiple posts
SELECT * FROM user_profiles.post_comments
WHERE post_id IN (/* id1, id2 */)
PER PARTITION LIMIT 2;
Example & guidance

If your endpoint needs the latest three items per user across many users, PER PARTITION LIMIT is the right tool. If you need three items total across many users, LIMIT plus client-side aggregation is required.

Key Takeaway

Select the limit type that matches the business requirement: per-group ceilings use PER PARTITION LIMIT; global ceilings use LIMIT plus aggregation.

screens.title: Secondary indexes: flexibility with costs
screens.narratorSegment: A secondary index allows you to query a table by a non-primary key column without using ALLOW FILTERING. For example, creating an index on the email column lets you run SELECT... WHERE email = 'alice@example. com' directly. That flexibility can be attractive, but secondary indexes have constraints and costs: they add write-time overhead because Cassandra must update the index on every replica; they can produce large index partitions for low-cardinality columns, and they may still scatter queries across nodes. Secondary indexes are most useful when the indexed column has moderate selectivity and you expect to retrieve only a small number of rows per query. For very common query patterns, the recommended Cassandra approach is denormalization: create a new table with a primary key designed for that query. For example, instead of frequently filtering by author_id, you might create blog_posts_by_author with author_id as the partition key. A misconception is to treat secondary indexes as a drop-in replacement for proper modeling; while convenient, they do not free you from thinking about cardinality and write costs. When in doubt, test with realistic write and read loads or choose a denormalized table for predictable production performance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Secondary Indexes
Definition

Secondary index basics

-- Create an index on email
CREATE INDEX ON user_profiles.users (email);

-- Then query by email without ALLOW FILTERING
SELECT * FROM user_profiles.users
WHERE email = 'alice.new@example.com';
  • Indexes speed development for occasional, low-volume lookups.
  • Indexes add write overhead because they are maintained on updates and deletes.
  • They are sensitive to the indexed column's cardinality and query selectivity.
Practical guidance

If the indexed column has few unique values, the index will generate large index partitions and degrade performance. If a query pattern is frequent or needs high throughput, prefer creating a new denormalized table keyed for that query.

Pro tip

Use secondary indexes for admin tools and low-traffic lookups. For application queries, model tables for the access pattern.

Next, execute a partition-targeted SELECT that retrieves the post you inserted earlier: SELECT title, content FROM blog_posts WHERE post_id = /* your_post_id */;. This targets a single partition and returns quickly. Then retrieve all comments for that post ordered by created time using the clustering column: SELECT comment_text, created_at FROM post_comments WHERE post_id = /* your_post_id */ ORDER BY comment_id DESC;. Then try the same query with ALLOW FILTERING and notice the warning about potential performance issues. Finally, create a secondary index on author_id and query again without ALLOW FILTERING to see how the index makes the query work. Throughout, compare execution time and think about whether an indexed lookup or a new table keyed by author_id is the correct long-term solution.

Then try the same query with ALLOW FILTERING and notice the warning about potential performance issues. Finally, create a secondary index on author_id and query again without ALLOW FILTERING to see how the index makes the query work. Throughout, compare execution time and think about whether an indexed lookup or a new table keyed by author_id is the correct long-term solution.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Hands-on Queries
Code Walkthrough

Sequence to run in the lab

1) Observe SELECT *
SELECT * FROM user_profiles.blog_posts;
2) Partition-targeted SELECT
SELECT title, content FROM user_profiles.blog_posts
WHERE post_id = /* your_post_id */;
3) Range on clustering column
SELECT comment_text, created_at FROM user_profiles.post_comments
WHERE post_id = /* your_post_id */
AND comment_id > minTimeuuid('2023-01-01')
AND comment_id < maxTimeuuid('2024-01-01');
Experiment & reflect
Try the non-key query and note the error, then add ALLOW FILTERING and observe the performance implications. Finally, create a secondary index on author_id and compare behavior and costs. 
-- Observe error
SELECT title FROM blog_posts WHERE author_id = /* id */;

-- With explicit override (risky)
SELECT title FROM blog_posts WHERE author_id = /* id */ ALLOW FILTERING;

-- Create an index
CREATE INDEX ON blog_posts (author_id);

-- Then query by author_id
SELECT title, publication_date FROM blog_posts WHERE author_id = /* id */;
Reflection

After testing, ask whether an index or a new table delivers predictable performance for your traffic pattern.

screens.title: Refactor challenge: from a costly query to a query-first table
screens.narratorSegment: In Cassandra the recommended long-term solution for a frequent query on a non-key column is to design a table that directly supports that query. This refactor challenge asks you to take a problematic query and propose a new table key. For example, suppose the application needs to fetch all posts by author_id frequently and the author_id is not part of the blog_posts primary key. Running SELECT title FROM blog_posts WHERE author_id = /* id */ either errors or requires ALLOW FILTERING and is unsafe. One option is a secondary index, but that has write overhead and cardinality concerns. The recommended approach is to create blog_posts_by_author with PRIMARY KEY (author_id, post_id) so author_id is the partition key and post_id (or publication_date) is a clustering column for ordering. This denormalization stores data twice but yields fast, predictable reads. When designing your refactor, list the query, expected read/write volume, and decide whether the write cost of denormalization is acceptable. A misconception is fearing denormalization because it duplicates data; in Cassandra, duplication is an explicit technique to optimize access patterns and maintain low latency at scale. What would you choose for a high-read, low-write workload?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Refactor Challenge
Architecture

Design a query-first table

Problematic query
-- Unsafe or slow
SELECT title FROM blog_posts WHERE author_id = /* id */;
This either errors or needs ALLOW FILTERING and is not safe for production. Consider expected query frequency and write amplification before choosing an approach.
Refactor: denormalized table
-- New table optimized for query
CREATE TABLE user_profiles.blog_posts_by_author (
  author_id uuid,
  post_id uuid,
  title text,
  publication_date timestamp,
  PRIMARY KEY (author_id, post_id)
);

-- Fast query
SELECT title, publication_date FROM user_profiles.blog_posts_by_author
WHERE author_id = /* id */;
Consider
  • Read vs write volume
  • Acceptable data duplication
  • Ordering needs (clustering columns)
Misconception
Duplication is not a bug in Cassandra; it's the standard way to support different query paths efficiently.
Check your design
List frequently used queries and make one table per heavy query pattern.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Key Concepts
SELECT & Partition Key
Full partition keys are required for efficient reads; avoid scanning partitions.
ORDER BY & Clustering
Order only by clustering columns within the partition and respect defined order.
ALLOW FILTERING
Use sparingly for ad-hoc queries; avoid in production because it forces wide scans.
LIMIT vs PER PARTITION LIMIT
LIMIT caps total rows; PER PARTITION LIMIT caps rows per partition when reading many partitions.
Secondary Index
Gives flexibility but increases write cost and depends on column cardinality; use with care.
Query-first modeling
When a query is common, create a denormalized table keyed for that query rather than relying on filtering.
Takeaway

Model for queries. Target partitions. Use indexes sparingly. Avoid ALLOW FILTERING in production.

Third, treat ALLOW FILTERING as an emergency override only and assess secondary indexes and denormalized tables as safer, long-term solutions for frequent query patterns. Carry these rules into your data modeling conversations: Cassandra favors predictable, partition-targeted reads over flexible, ad-hoc filtering at scale. Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › What to Remember
Target partitions
Provide the full partition key for efficient reads and lower latency.
Order carefully
ORDER BY works only on clustering columns in their defined order.
Avoid ad-hoc filtering
Use ALLOW FILTERING only for small, ad-hoc checks; prefer denormalization for production queries.
Final thought

Model your data around the queries your application actually needs. That is Cassandra's design principle and your path to predictable performance.

fullNarratorScript:
Retrieving data is the most frequent operation in many applications, and Cassandra uses the SELECT statement for this purpose. But although CQL looks like S Q L, its execution model is different: every efficient query must be expressed around the primary key so the cluster knows which partitions to read. In this lesson you will learn core SELECT patterns: why you should avoid table scans, how the WHERE clause ties to partition and clustering keys, when ORDER BY is allowed, and the real cost of ALLOW FILTERING. I will show concrete CQL examples and practical guidance you can apply immediately when modeling tables. You will also see how LIMIT and PER PARTITION LIMIT behave differently, and where a secondary index might help — and when it will hurt. By the end you should be comfortable writing SELECT statements that return only the data you need without destabilizing the cluster. A quick question to hold while we dive in: when you request rows without a partition key, what costs do you expect the coordinator node to bear?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to compose efficient SELECT statements in Cassandra and explain why primary keys drive query performance. You will learn to construct SELECTs that use full partition keys to target partitions directly, and to filter on clustering columns in their defined order. You will also recognize when ALLOW FILTERING is unsafe and when a secondary index or a new table is the better option. Finally, you will practice ordering and limiting results with ORDER BY, LIMIT, and PER PARTITION LIMIT to retrieve top-N results predictably. Each objective maps to a competency milestone so you can verify that your queries are both correct and production-safe. We will practice with the blog_posts and post_comments examples repeatedly, so you can see the difference between ad-hoc filtering and query-driven modeling. As you work, ask: does this query require scanning partitions, and if so, how could the schema change to avoid that scan?

This second objectives slide focuses on applied skills you will practice in the hands-on activity. You will learn to use clustering column filters with range operators to implement time-window queries, for example retrieving comments within a date range. You will practice LIMIT and PER PARTITION LIMIT to fetch top-N results per group, which is useful for leaderboards or retrieving the most recent items per partition. You will also explore secondary indexes: creating them and evaluating when they help versus when designing a dedicated table is a better trade-off. Finally, you will reflect on denormalization: Cassandra expects you to model tables around query patterns, so we will include a refactor challenge where you propose a new table key when a query pattern is common and costly. These skills together let you turn a problematic query into a production-safe data model.

A SELECT statement in Cassandra may look like S Q L, but its performance characteristics are different because data is partitioned across nodes. The simplest form, SELECT * FROM keyspace. table, returns every column and every row unless you constrain it. In distributed clusters this causes a full table scan: each node must contribute rows and the coordinator collects and streams them, which can saturate network and C P U. For this reason, production queries should never use SELECT * across large tables. Instead, pick the columns you need and provide a partition key so Cassandra targets a single partition. For example, selecting a blog post by its post_id is efficient because the coordinator reads only that partition: SELECT title, content FROM user_profiles. blog_posts WHERE post_id = /* your_post_id */; A common misconception is that SELECT * is harmless for infrequent queries; in reality the coordinator can still touch many nodes and lead to timeouts. Another subtle point is that selecting fewer columns reduces payload size and lowers read amplification. As a practical rule, design your application query to return only the fields required for the user story. Reflect: if a query must scan many partitions, how would you remodel the data to avoid that scan?

The WHERE clause in CQL is tightly coupled to the primary key. Cassandra requires the full partition key to be present in the WHERE clause for efficient queries; without it, the coordinator cannot narrow the read to a known partition and will either fail or require ALLOW FILTERING. Think of the partition key as the address of a house in a distributed neighborhood: you must give the house number to fetch its contents quickly. You can filter on clustering columns after supplying the partition key, and clustering filters must follow the column order defined in the table schema. Supported operators include equality, IN for multiple partition values, and range operators for clustering columns. For example, selecting comments for a post by post_id is correct, and you can apply a time range on the clustering comment_id using > and minTimeuuid('2023-01-01') AND comment_id < maxTimeuuid('2024-01-01'); A frequent misconception is that IN on a partition key is always free; while IN lets you read multiple partitions, it causes multiple partition reads and may still be expensive if many partitions are involved. Ask yourself: am I targeting a small, bounded set of partitions, or am I requesting a broad scan?

ALLOW FILTERING lets you override Cassandra's protections and run queries that would otherwise error because they require scanning multiple partitions or filtering non-key columns. It does what it promises: it forces the coordinator to collect candidate rows from replicas and apply the filter in memory or on the coordinator, but that comes at a cost — increased network traffic, coordinator C P U load, and unpredictable latency. Use ALLOW FILTERING only for ad-hoc investigation or administrative checks on small tables. For application queries, prefer modelling your data for the required access pattern or using a secondary index when appropriate. A concrete example: querying users by city with ALLOW FILTERING will work but can scan many partitions. Better approaches include adding city to the primary key of a denormalized table used specifically for that query, or creating a carefully chosen secondary index when cardinality is suitable. A persistent misconception is to accept occasional slow queries with ALLOW FILTERING; in real deployments, occasional slow queries often become consistent problems under load. Before adding ALLOW FILTERING, ask whether a schema change or index would serve the query safely.

ORDER BY in Cassandra is intentionally limited: you can only sort by clustering columns and the order must respect the clustering order defined when the table was created. This restriction exists because data within a partition is physically stored according to clustering order; Cassandra can sort efficiently inside that partition, but it cannot sort across partitions without a coordination-heavy shuffle. For example, ordering post_comments by comment_id descending is valid if the clustering column is comment_id and the table's clustering order allows it: SELECT comment_text, created_at FROM user_profiles. post_comments WHERE post_id = /* id */ ORDER BY comment_id DESC; If you try to order by a non-clustering column or by a clustering column out of its defined sequence, Cassandra will return an error. A common misconception is that ORDER BY will reorganize results globally; instead, it only guarantees order within a single partition. If your application needs global ordering across partitions, you must implement an application-side aggregator or design a table keyed to the ordering you need. Consider whether you can limit results per partition and then merge them in the application, or refactor the schema for the target query.

LIMIT and PER PARTITION LIMIT let you bound the number of rows returned by a SELECT, but they serve different needs. LIMIT restricts the total number of rows in the result set, so when you query a single partition, LIMIT provides a simple top-N behavior. PER PARTITION LIMIT is specifically useful when a query touches multiple partitions, for example when you use IN on the partition key. PER PARTITION LIMIT guarantees at most N rows per partition, which helps ensure fair representation across partitions and prevents one large partition from dominating results. For example, SELECT * FROM user_profiles. post_comments WHERE post_id IN (id1, id2) PER PARTITION LIMIT 2 returns at most two comments for each post. A misconception is to treat PER PARTITION LIMIT as a global LIMIT; it is not. Also remember that combining ORDER BY with LIMIT works within a partition to return the top N in the requested order. When designing APIs, choose which of these limits matches the user story: a single global top-N across many partitions requires additional client-side aggregation, while PER PARTITION LIMIT keeps pagination predictable and partition-local.

A secondary index allows you to query a table by a non-primary key column without using ALLOW FILTERING. For example, creating an index on the email column lets you run SELECT... WHERE email = 'alice@example. com' directly. That flexibility can be attractive, but secondary indexes have constraints and costs: they add write-time overhead because Cassandra must update the index on every replica; they can produce large index partitions for low-cardinality columns, and they may still scatter queries across nodes. Secondary indexes are most useful when the indexed column has moderate selectivity and you expect to retrieve only a small number of rows per query. For very common query patterns, the recommended Cassandra approach is denormalization: create a new table with a primary key designed for that query. For example, instead of frequently filtering by author_id, you might create blog_posts_by_author with author_id as the partition key. A misconception is to treat secondary indexes as a drop-in replacement for proper modeling; while convenient, they do not free you from thinking about cardinality and write costs. When in doubt, test with realistic write and read loads or choose a denormalized table for predictable production performance.

This targets a single partition and returns quickly. Then retrieve all comments for that post ordered by created time using the clustering column: SELECT comment_text, created_at FROM post_comments WHERE post_id = /* your_post_id */ ORDER BY comment_id DESC;.
